mcqs.question: What three design levers define most production time-series designs, according to the answer skeleton?
options: Replicating every write synchronously, sharding by user ID, and caching the most recent point
Using the newest available database engine, minimizing the number of columns, and normalizing every relationship
Partitioning by time range, writing append-only, and downsampling old data instead of keeping full resolution forever
Storing all data in a single unpartitioned table and relying entirely on read replicas for scale
mcqs.explanation: Time-based partitioning, append-only writes, and downsampling older data together define the shape of most production time-series systems, regardless of the specific database. User-ID sharding, engine novelty, column minimization, and unpartitioned storage don't address the actual access pattern.

mcqs.question: What does a purpose-built time-series or wide-column store provide natively that a generic relational table typically requires manual work to achieve?
options: The ability to store more than one numeric column per row
Support for foreign key constraints between related tables
Native TTL/retention policies and optimized time-range scans, instead of hand-built indexing and deletion jobs
The ability to run any SQL query at all against stored data
mcqs.explanation: Purpose-built stores provide time-range scans and retention/rollup as first-class, optimized operations, where a generic relational table needs custom indexing and manual deletion jobs to approximate the same behavior. Multiple numeric columns and foreign keys aren't the differentiator here, and many time-series stores do support SQL-like querying.

mcqs.question: Why is a downsampling and retention schedule considered a largely one-way decision?
options: Once raw, fine-grained data is deleted after being rolled up, that resolution generally can't be reconstructed later
Downsampling policies can be reversed automatically at any time with no data loss
It only applies to data stored in cloud object storage, not databases
Retention schedules are enforced permanently by government regulation in every industry
mcqs.explanation: Once the raw points behind a rollup are deleted, that fine-grained resolution is gone for good — the decision is effectively permanent at that point. It isn't automatically reversible, isn't specific to object storage, and isn't a universal regulatory requirement.

mcqs.question: Why is storing time-series data at full resolution forever in a generic relational table a pitfall, even if storage itself is cheap?
options: Relational databases cannot technically store timestamped numeric data at all
Full-resolution storage is illegal for most types of metrics data under data protection law
It requires switching database vendors entirely before any data can be queried
Query performance degrades as the unbounded table grows, since generic tables lack built-in rollup or expiration, and every range query pays the cost of scanning the full accumulated history
mcqs.explanation: The real cost is query performance, not just storage price — an ever-growing table with no native rollup or expiration makes every time-range query progressively more expensive. Relational databases can absolutely store timestamped data, there's no such blanket legal restriction, and no vendor switch is inherently required.
